sheet.howExamined: B1 Higher, 1 hour, 70 marks, calculator allowed. Outcome 1.6.4 is Higher Tier only. It arrives as a labelled diagram: name the structures [1] each, name and describe the synapse [2], and an explanation of [2]-[3] about the speed of the response. It is also natural QWC material, because the pathway supplies six or seven indicative points in a fixed order. steps.working: The heat is the stimulus. A receptor in the skin detects it and produces nerve impulses.
steps.decision: Start at the stimulus and name the receptor. The outcome's first bullet is the receptor 'that detects stimuli and produces nerve impulses', so both halves are worth writing.

steps.working: The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the spinal cord.
steps.decision: Name the neurone and say where it goes. 'A nerve' is not enough — there are three different neurones and each has its own mark.

steps.working: It crosses a synapse to the association neurone inside the spinal cord.
steps.decision: Mention the synapse here rather than leaving it to a later part. CCEA's bullet puts the neurones and the synapses in the same sentence.

whyMenu.explain: The outcome says the three neurones are 'connected by synapses (gaps between neurones)', so the gaps are part of the pathway, not an optional extra.

steps.working: It crosses a second synapse to the motor neurone, which carries it out of the spinal cord.
steps.decision: Two synapses, not one. The second is the one candidates forget, and it is often the difference between four marks and five.

steps.working: The motor neurone carries the impulse to the effector — a muscle in the arm — which contracts and pulls the hand away.
steps.decision: Finish at the effector and name it as a muscle. The response is what the muscle does, not the body part that moves.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The heat is the stimulus; a receptor in the skin detects it and produces nerve impulses. options.feedback: A gap, crossed by a chemical. Summer 2024 examiners reported that fewer candidates could answer the synapse question than could name the neurones.

items.stem: How many synapses are there in a spinal reflex arc made of three neurones?

options.feedback: One on each side of the association neurone. Three neurones, two joins.
One synapse would only join two neurones. There are three in this pathway, so there are two gaps.
Three neurones have two gaps between them, not three — the same as three fence posts having two gaps.

options.feedback: The neurones do not touch. Every junction between two of them is a synapse.

items.stem: Why would a pathway with more synapses give a slower response?
items.skill: Explain the delay at a synapse

options.text: At each gap a chemical must be released and diffuse across, which takes time
options.feedback: The mechanism, not just the outcome. March 2026 examiners said most candidates knew it was slower but fewer explained why.

options.text: The impulse has further to travel
options.feedback: The gaps are microscopic, so the extra distance is nothing. It is the chemical crossing that takes the time.

options.text: The impulse gets weaker at each gap
options.feedback: A new impulse of the same size is started in the next neurone. What is lost is time, not strength.
Energy is not what the question is about. The delay comes from diffusion across each gap.

The receptor detects the stimulus. Co-ordinating means deciding what happens next.
The effector carries out the response at the end of the pathway.

parts.stem:
A reflex pathway contains two synapses. A different pathway, of the same length, contains six.
Explain which response will be slower, and why.

accepted: the pathway with six synapses is slower because a chemical has to diffuse across each gap and that takes time

scheme.for: the pathway with six synapses is slower
because at each synapse a chemical has to be released and diffuse across the gap
and diffusion is slower than an impulse travelling along a neurone, so each extra gap adds a delay
scheme.examinerNote: March 2026: most candidates said slower but fewer explained why.

hints: Say which is slower first, then explain what happens at each gap.
The two pathways are the same length, so distance is not the answer.
parts.workedSolution: The pathway with six synapses is slower. At every synapse the impulse cannot cross the gap directly: the first neurone releases a chemical, which has to diffuse across before a new impulse starts. Diffusion across a gap is slower than conduction along a neurone, so each of the six gaps adds a delay, and six delays take longer than two.

commonErrors.feedback: The stem says both pathways are the same length, so distance cannot be the reason. The delay is the chemical diffusing across each gap.

parts.workedSolution: The sharp stone is the stimulus. A receptor in the skin of the foot detects it and produces nerve impulses. The impulses travel along the sensory neurone to the spinal cord, where they cross a synapse to the association neurone, and then a second synapse to the motor neurone. The motor neurone carries the impulses to the effector, a muscle in the leg, which contracts and lifts the foot. The response is fast because the reflex is co-ordinated by the spinal cord rather than the brain, so the pathway is short and contains only two synapses, and because it is automatic — no conscious decision is needed, so the foot moves before the pain is felt.

commonErrors.feedback: The association neurone is missing, and with it one of the seven indicative points and usually one of the synapses too. The pathway has three neurones, not two.

findTheMistake.stem:
Conall is asked: 'Describe the pathway of a spinal reflex arc from stimulus to response. [5]'
His answer:
studentWorking: The stimulus is detected by a receptor.
The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the brain.
The brain decides what to do and sends the impulse to the motor neurone.
The motor neurone carries it to the hand, which moves.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: In a **spinal** reflex the impulse goes to the spinal cord, not the brain, and it is the **association neurone** inside the cord that links the sensory neurone to the motor neurone. Routing the impulse through the brain also loses the two synapses, and line 4 names the hand rather than the muscle as the effector.
correction: The stimulus is detected by a receptor, which produces nerve impulses.
The impulse travels along the sensory neurone to the spinal cord.
It crosses a synapse to the association neurone, then a second synapse to the motor neurone.
The motor neurone carries it to the effector, a muscle, which contracts to produce the response.
findTheMistake.feedback: One mark from five: the receptor is right. Everything after it follows from one wrong turn at line 2, which is worth noticing — a single misremembered word can cost four marks rather than one. Two habits fix it. First, the word *spinal* in the question names the structure that co-ordinates the response. Second, count the neurones as you write: three of them, with a synapse between each pair, and an effector that is always a muscle or a gland.

prompts.answer: The spinal cord. The impulse does not have to travel to the brain and no conscious decision is made, so the pathway is short and the response is quick.

prompts.prompt: What does a receptor do, in the specification's words?
prompts.answer: It detects stimuli in the environment and produces nerve impulses.
